text: Your vital lung capacity falls by roughly 200 ml each decade from your twenties on — by 70, most people are down to about 75% of what they had at 30. Posture affects how well you use what's left: in a study of healthy young men, simply holding a forward-head position measurably reduced inspiratory muscle strength. Keeping your ribcage and upper back mobile supports the mechanics of a full breath.
source: Wang et al., Frontiers in Immunology, 2024 (ageing-lung review); Zafar et al., BioMed Research International, 2018 (n=15)

text: About 28-35% of adults over 65 fall each year, rising to 32-42% for those over 70. Falls are the leading cause of injury death in older adults, and many are preventable. Stretching reliably improves joint range of motion, and one trial found hip and ankle stretching improved walking speed in older adults. Balance and strength training have the strongest fall-prevention evidence, so pair your stretching with both.
source: WHO, Global Report on Falls Prevention in Older Age, 2007; Sadaqa et al., Frontiers in Public Health, 2023; Christiansen, Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2008 (n=37)

text: Kyphosis — that rounded upper back — can be improved. In a six-month randomised trial of adults aged 60 and over, spine-strengthening and posture training reduced the curve by about 3 degrees compared with a control group, and participants felt better about their appearance.
source: Katzman et al., Osteoporosis International, 2017 (randomised controlled trial, n=99)

text: Adults are sedentary for 10 or more hours a day, and office workers spend roughly three-quarters of their working hours sitting. People who sit more than seven hours a day average about 6 degrees less hip extension than people who sit little. The encouraging part: consistent stretching reliably improves that range, and much of the gain comes from your nervous system raising its tolerance rather than from tissue permanently lengthening.
source: Boukabache et al., Musculoskeletal Science and Practice, 2021; Diaz et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017; Parry & Straker, BMC Public Health, 2013

text: Muscle stiffness isn't only about the muscle — much of it is your nervous system. Reviewing the stretching literature, researchers found that the gains from a single session, or from a 3-to-8-week program, come mostly from increased tolerance to the stretch sensation rather than from tissue permanently lengthening.
source: Weppler & Magnusson, Physical Therapy, 2010

text: Balance isn't a talent — it's a skill that fades without practice. Among adults aged 51 to 75, those who couldn't hold a 10-second one-legged stance had about 1.8 times the risk of dying over the next seven years, even after accounting for age, sex, BMI and existing illness. The good news: balance responds well to regular practice.
source: Araujo et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022; Chen et al., PLoS One, 2026 (dose-response meta-analysis)

text: Grip strength predicts all-cause mortality better than systolic blood pressure. Every 5-kilogram decrease in grip strength is associated with a 16% higher risk of death from any cause. It's not that squeezing a hand towel makes you live longer on its own — grip is a window into whole-body strength, and strength is the window into how well you age.
source: Leong et al., The Lancet, 2015 (PURE study, 139,691 adults across 17 countries)

text: Getting down to the floor and back up without your hands tests leg strength, flexibility and balance at once. In a study of 2,002 Brazilian adults aged 51 to 80, each extra point on a 10-point sit-and-rise score went with about 21% better survival over roughly six years, and the lowest scorers had about five times the mortality of the highest.
source: Brito et al., European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 2014 (retrospective cohort, n=2,002)

text: Complex movement patterns — ones that coordinate many joints and muscle groups — are associated with better-preserved thinking in older adults. They aren't the only route: in a year-long trial of adults aged 62 to 79, coordination training and brisk walking each improved attention compared with a control group, apparently through different brain networks.
source: Voelcker-Rehage & Niemann, Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 2013; Voelcker-Rehage, Godde & Staudinger, Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 2011

text: Frozen shoulder — adhesive capsulitis — affects about 2 to 5% of people. People with diabetes are around five times more likely to develop it, and thyroid disease raises the risk too. It usually improves over one to two years, though some people are left with stiffness that lasts.
source: Ramirez, American Family Physician, 2019

text: Low back pain is the world's leading cause of years lived with disability, and most adults will have it at some point. For acute back pain, Cochrane evidence shows staying active gives a small advantage over bed rest, and guidelines no longer recommend prolonged bed rest.
source: GBD 2019 Diseases and Injuries Collaborators, Lancet, 2020; Walker, Journal of Spinal Disorders, 2000; Dahm et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2010

text: In a study of more than 3,000 adults aged 70 to 79, those with the weakest thigh (knee-extensor) strength were about twice as likely to develop difficulty walking or climbing stairs over the next two and a half years as the strongest. Rising from a chair without your hands is a practical way to keep working those muscles.
source: Visser et al., Journals of Gerontology: Series A, 2005 (Health ABC, n=3,075)

text: Your upper back is built to rotate and extend, and sitting appears to cost some of that: in 92 young adults, those sitting more than seven hours a day had about 14% less thoracic rotation than physically active peers (65 degrees versus 75).
source: Heneghan et al., BMJ Open, 2018 (n=92)

text: Your calf muscles act as a 'second heart', squeezing the leg veins to push blood back toward the chest when you walk. In a randomised trial of people with chronic venous insufficiency, a structured calf-strengthening program measurably improved that pump after six months.
source: Padberg et al., Journal of Vascular Surgery, 2004 (randomised, n=31); Araujo et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2016

text: Breathing at about six breaths a minute — far slower than most of us ever breathe — reliably raises heart rate variability, the standard marker of vagal, rest-and-digest activity. A 2022 review pooled 223 studies and found it during the session, straight after a single session, and after weeks of practice.
source: Laborde et al., Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 2022 (meta-analysis, 223 studies); de Freitas Gonçalves et al., Health Science Reports, 2022 (22 studies, 17,214 people)

text: Vagal traffic to the heart peaks on the out-breath — which is why your pulse quickens a little as you breathe in and settles as you breathe out, and why long exhales feel calming. In the best-designed trials, it is the slow pace that appears to do most of the work.
source: Farmer et al., Journal of Physiology, 2016 (brainstem mechanism, animal study); Meehan et al., Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback, 2024 (two randomised experiments); Bae et al., Psychophysiology, 2021

text: Five minutes a day of cyclic sighing — two inhales through the nose, then one long slow exhale — improved mood and slowed resting breathing more than five minutes of mindfulness meditation did, over a month, in a randomised study of 108 people.
source: Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2023 (randomised, n=108, 4 weeks)

text: Nostril-regulated breathing does slow the heart: a 2026 meta-analysis of seven trials in 683 people with high blood pressure found a consistent drop in heart rate. Compared head to head, left- and right-nostril practices produced the same changes, and the breathing rate fell either way.
source: Chidambaram et al., Indian Heart Journal, 2026 (7 RCTs, 683 people); Telles et al., International Journal of Yoga, 2024 (randomised crossover, n=47)

text: Breathing through the nose does something mouth-breathing does not: the airflow paces electrical rhythms in the brain's memory and emotion centres. Recordings made inside the brains of eight epilepsy patients found those rhythms tracking the breath — and fading when breathing was diverted to the mouth. It is the airflow itself that carries the signal, not extra oxygen.
source: Zelano et al., Journal of Neuroscience, 2016 (intracranial recordings, n=8; behavioural tasks, n=62 and n=33)

text: Pursed-lip breathing — in through the nose, out slowly through pursed lips — is a clinical technique for breathlessness rather than a relaxation fad. In COPD trials it reduces the trapped air that makes the next breath harder to take.
source: Cabral et al., European Journal of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine, 2015 (randomised crossover, n=40); de Araujo et al., Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine, 2015 (n=25)

text: Eight weeks of daily diaphragmatic breathing lowered cortisol and improved sustained attention in forty healthy adults. The direction matches the rest of this evidence — slow breathing shifts autonomic state.
source: Ma et al., Frontiers in Psychology, 2017 (n=40, quasi-randomised, no active control)

text: The 4-7-8 pattern is a simple way to slow your breathing right down. Slow breathing raises heart rate variability, a sign your body is shifting into its calmer rest-and-digest mode. In one study of healthy young adults, heart rate and systolic blood pressure dropped right after a few rounds of 4-7-8.
source: Vierra et al., Physiological Reports, 2022 (n=43); Marchant et al., Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback, 2025 (n=84)

text: A Cochrane review of 27 trials in adults with neck pain found that strength training for the neck, shoulder and shoulder-blade muscles eased long-lasting neck pain.
source: Gross et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2015 (27 RCTs, n=2,485)

text: A 2024 review pooled 8 trials of office workers with chronic neck pain. Strengthening the neck, shoulder and shoulder-blade muscles reduced neck pain and disability compared with control groups.
source: Jones et al., Applied Ergonomics, 2024 (meta-analysis of 8 RCTs)

text: In the CSAW trial, 313 people with at least three months of shoulder pain — despite exercise therapy and a steroid injection — got decompression surgery, placebo keyhole surgery, or no treatment. At six months, real surgery did no better than the placebo. Both surgeries beat no treatment slightly, but not by a clinically important amount.
source: Beard et al., Lancet, 2018 (randomised placebo-controlled trial, n=313)

text: A Cochrane review of exercise for hand osteoarthritis found small improvements in hand pain, function and finger stiffness right after the programmes (pain pooled from 5 trials, 381 people).
source: Østerås et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2017 (systematic review of RCTs, n=381)

text: Exercise can ease hip osteoarthritis. A 2026 Cochrane review of 18 trials (1,368 people) found that, compared with no treatment or usual care, land-based exercise probably reduces pain and improves physical function slightly.
source: Hall et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2026 (18 RCTs, n=1,368)

text: Your hip abductors are the muscles on the outside of your hip. An Australian study followed 952 adults aged 65 and over for a median of 11.5 years: those with stronger hip abductors were less likely to need emergency care after a fall.
source: Yosef et al., Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, 2026 (prospective cohort, n=952)

text: A 2024 Cochrane review of 139 trials (12,468 people with knee osteoarthritis) found land-based exercise probably improves pain and physical function in the short term compared with control groups, and no single type of exercise stood out.
source: Lawford et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2024 (139 RCTs, n=12,468)

text: Strength can still be built very late in life. In a 10-week trial, 100 frail nursing-home residents (average age 87, range 72 to 98) were randomised. Those doing high-intensity resistance training increased muscle strength by 113% on average, versus 3% in non-exercisers, and walked faster.
source: Fiatarone et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 1994 (RCT, n=100)

text: How long should you hold a hamstring stretch? In a trial of 62 adults aged 65 to 97 with tight hamstrings, stretching five days a week for six weeks, 60-second holds gained range of motion faster than 30- or 15-second holds, and the gain lasted longer after stopping.
source: Feland et al., Physical Therapy, 2001 (RCT, n=62)

text: A Cochrane review pooled 108 trials of exercise in people aged 60 and over living in the community. Exercise cut the rate of falls by 23%, and programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises did about the same (24%). The authors rate these falls results high-certainty.
source: Sherrington et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2019 (108 RCTs, n=23,407)

text: A 2017 review of 18 randomised trials (3,824 older adults) found tai chi groups had fewer people falling and a lower rate of falls than control groups, and the benefit looked larger with more frequent practice.
source: Huang et al., BMJ Open, 2017 (meta-analysis of 18 RCTs, n=3,824)

text: A 2022 meta-analysis of cohort studies found adults who did muscle-strengthening activities had about a 10-17% lower risk of death from any cause than those who did none. The biggest reduction came at roughly 30 to 60 minutes a week.
source: Momma et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022 (meta-analysis of cohort studies)

text: A study that followed 312 people aged 60 to 90 for a year found that those who fell had weaker big-toe and lesser-toe flexor muscles than those who did not. The authors suggest toe-strengthening may help.
source: Mickle et al., Clinical Biomechanics, 2009 (prospective cohort, n=312)

text: In a 10-year study of 1,104 male firefighters (mean age 39.6), men who could do more than 40 push-ups at the start had far fewer later heart and blood-vessel events than men who managed fewer than 10.
source: Yang et al., JAMA Network Open, 2019 (retrospective cohort, n=1,104)

text: In a trial, 18 young men trained twice a week for 8 weeks with either a light-load bench press or push-ups adjusted (for example, kneeling) to match that load. Both groups got stronger and built thicker chest and triceps muscles, with similar results.
source: Kikuchi et al., Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness, 2017 (randomised trial, n=18)

text: Researchers used motion sensors on 50 adults without shoulder pain, grouped by whether their pectoralis minor — a small muscle beneath the main chest muscle — was relatively short or long. When they raised an arm, the short group's shoulder blade stayed tipped forward more, a pattern earlier studies saw in shoulder impingement.
source: Borstad & Ludewig, Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, 2005 (cross-sectional, n=50)

text: Twenty-five people with shoulder pain and 25 without did a daily home stretch for the pectoralis minor, a chest muscle, for six weeks. The shoulder-pain group reported less pain and better arm function.
source: Rosa et al., Journal of Hand Therapy, 2017 (parallel-group intervention, n=50)

text: A large Cochrane review pooled 249 trials of exercise for adults whose low back pain had lasted over 12 weeks. Exercise probably reduced pain compared with no treatment or usual care, by an amount the authors judged clinically important. Day-to-day function improved too.
source: Hayden et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2021 (systematic review of 249 RCTs)

text: A review of 21 trials in over 30,000 people looked at ways to prevent low back pain. Exercise combined with education lowered the chance of a new episode. Education alone, back belts and shoe insoles did not appear to prevent it.
source: Steffens et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2016 (meta-analysis of 21 RCTs, n=30,850)

text: In a trial of 447 office workers, one weekly hour of dumbbell strength training for the neck and shoulders — including reverse flies and shrugs — reduced neck and shoulder pain over 20 weeks compared with no training. Splitting the hour into one, three or nine sessions worked about equally well.
source: Andersen et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2012 (cluster randomised trial, n=447)

text: In a trial of 47 office workers with long-lasting neck and shoulder pain, 10 weeks of shoulder-blade training reduced pain more than no training, by an amount the authors call clinically relevant.
source: Andersen et al., Journal of Occupational Rehabilitation, 2014 (randomised controlled trial, n=47)

text: A review of 24 studies in adults aged 45 and over with a rounded upper back found that exercise or physical therapy modestly improved the curve. It also showed small gains in quality of life, pain and back-muscle strength. No serious side effects were reported.
source: Ponzano et al., Archives of Osteoporosis, 2021 (meta-analysis of 24 studies)

text: In 93 adults aged 21 to 39 with tight hamstrings, holding a hamstring stretch for 30 seconds, five days a week for six weeks, improved range as much as holding it for 60 seconds, and stretching three times a day did no better than once. All the stretching groups beat no stretching.
source: Bandy et al., Physical Therapy, 1997 (randomised controlled trial, n=93)

text: A review of 12 prospective studies (5,459 people, mostly followed for a year) found that restricted hamstring range of motion was linked to a higher chance of developing low back pain, and so were reduced side-bending and a flatter lower-back curve.
source: Sadler et al., BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders, 2017 (review of prospective cohorts, n=5,459)

text: Neck pain is one of the most common aches there is. The Global Burden of Disease study estimated that 203 million people worldwide had it in 2020, with rates higher in women and peaking between ages 45 and 74.
source: GBD 2021 Neck Pain Collaborators, Lancet Rheumatology, 2024 (modelling study, 92 data sources)

text: Deep neck flexor training is gentle work on the small muscles at the front of the neck. A review of 12 trials (502 people with persistent neck pain) found strong evidence it improves coordination between the deep and surface neck muscles, and it improved head and neck posture.
source: Blomgren et al., BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders, 2018 (systematic review of 12 RCTs, n=502)

text: In the GRASP trial, 708 adults with a new episode of rotator cuff shoulder pain got either up to six supervised physio exercise sessions or one session of advice plus a home programme. Over 12 months, pain and function didn't differ between the two, and a steroid injection gave no long-term benefit.
source: Hopewell et al., Lancet, 2021 (randomised controlled trial, n=708)

text: How much shoulder movement do everyday tasks need? A review of 36 studies of people without impairments, performing 66 daily tasks, found roughly 130 degrees of lifting the arm forward or out to the side was needed.
source: Oosterwijk et al., Physiotherapy Theory and Practice, 2018 (systematic review of 36 studies)

text: In a trial of 96 healthy older adults, those taught a hip flexor stretch to do at home twice a day for 10 weeks gained a modest amount of hip extension compared with a group who stretched their shoulders.
source: Kerrigan et al., Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2003 (randomised controlled trial, n=96)

text: A review pooling 14 trials of 673 people with pain around the kneecap found that adding hip strengthening to knee strengthening reduced pain and improved activity more than knee exercises alone, and the benefit lasted beyond the training period.
source: Nascimento et al., Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, 2018 (meta-analysis of 14 trials, n=673)

text: A study of 566 adults aged 20 to 81 tested single-leg heel raises to fatigue and found the test very repeatable week to week. Overall, men did more than women (a median of 24 versus 21), but over age 60 women outperformed men. Age, sex, body weight and activity level all shaped the result.
source: Hébert-Losier et al., Physiotherapy, 2017 (cross-sectional, n=566)

text: A review of 8 randomised trials of stretching for plantar fasciitis (heel pain) found that stretching the sole of the foot directly reduced pain more than calf stretching. Calf stretching, alone or combined, beat sham stretching.
source: Siriphorn et al., Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies, 2020 (meta-analysis of 8 RCTs)

text: A review of 30 trials (2,123 people) with tennis elbow — pain on the outer elbow — found exercise did better than passive care, wait-and-see or steroid injections, and against injections the gains in pain-free grip strength held up long term.
source: Karanasios et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2021 (meta-analysis of 30 RCTs, n=2,123)

text: A Cochrane review of 121 trials (6,700 older adults) found that progressive resistance training, usually two to three times a week, had a large effect on muscle strength and a moderate to large effect on getting up from a chair, plus a smaller gain in walking speed. Serious problems were rare.
source: Liu & Latham, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2009 (121 RCTs, n=6,700)

text: In a trial, 32 adults around age 70 were randomly assigned to nine weeks of core exercises that also challenged balance, or to a control group. The core group gained trunk strength and spinal mobility and did better on walking and reaching balance tests, and attendance was high.
source: Granacher et al., Gerontology, 2013 (randomised controlled trial, n=32)

text: Office workers with long-lasting neck pain who did simple neck and shoulder stretches twice a day, five days a week, had less pain after just four weeks than workers who only got ergonomics advice: about 1.4 points more improvement on a 0-10 scale, plus better neck function.
source: Tunwattanapong et al., Clinical Rehabilitation, 2016 (randomised controlled trial, n=96)

text: Short movement breaks may ease the aches of long sitting. A 2026 review of six small trials (210 people in total) found that in four of them, breaks of 2 to 10 minutes (stretching, light exercise or stair climbing) reduced discomfort more than sitting still or resting.
source: Zeng et al., BMC Public Health, 2026 (systematic review of 6 RCTs, n=210)

text: Which exercises help a sore back most? A review of 118 trials (9,710 adults with long-lasting low back pain) found that core-based exercise and Pilates ranked among the most effective for reducing both pain and disability. Programmes of 3 to 9 weeks did best.
source: Fernández-Rodríguez et al., Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, 2022 (network meta-analysis of 118 RCTs, n=9,710)
